title: Algorithms to Live By: The Computer Science of Human Decisions
author: Brian Christian and Tom Griffiths
target_audience: General readers interested in science and technology
People looking to improve personal and professional decision-making
Fans of applied mathematics and cognitive science
Students and practitioners of computer science
Anyone curious about everyday problem-solving techniques
core_themes: Application of computer science algorithms to real-life problems
Limits of rationality and the role of computational tradeoffs
primary_purpose: To demonstrate how classic computer science algorithms can inform, guide, and improve the everyday decisions people make, from prioritizing tasks and organizing information to finding a spouse or choosing when to stop searching for a solution.

structure_format.narrative_style: Engaging, explanatory, and story-driven with accessible analogies
structure_format.organization: Divided into chapters, each exploring a specific class of algorithms (e.g., sorting, caching, scheduling, networking)
features: Explanations of technical concepts in lay terms

key_concepts_lessons: Optimal Stopping: The 37% Rule for knowing when to stop searching and make a choice.
Explore/Exploit Tradeoff: Balancing new opportunities versus sticking with the known.
Sorting and Filtering: Organizing information efficiently to improve clarity and reduce decision fatigue.
Caching and Memory: Prioritizing what information to keep accessible, inspired by how computers manage memory.
Scheduling and Queues: Managing time, priorities, and multitasking using proven computational strategies.
Overfitting and Generalization: Avoiding excessive customization or rigid rules in decision making.
Randomness and Probabilistic Thinking: Embracing luck and uncertainty in outcomes.
Game Theory and Cooperation: Applying strategic reasoning to social and competitive situations.
notable_features: Translates advanced computer science concepts into practical life advice
Uses engaging stories and analogies from diverse fields
Bridges psychology, math, and computer science
Highlights the universal relevance of algorithmic thinking
cultural_historical_context: Published in the mid-2010s during a period of growing public interest in data-driven living, artificial intelligence, and behavioral economics. The book positioned computer science principles as tools for not just machines, but also humans navigating complex modern life.
reception_impact: Critically acclaimed for originality and clarity
Helped popularize algorithmic thinking outside tech circles
Widely cited in productivity and decision science discussions
Became influential among knowledge workers, educators, and enthusiasts of rational living
comparable_titles: Thinking, Fast and Slow by Daniel Kahneman
Superforecasting by Philip E. Tetlock and Dan Gardner
How Not to Be Wrong: The Power of Mathematical Thinking by Jordan Ellenberg
The Art of Strategy by Avinash K. Dixit and Barry J. Nalebuff
